title: Zink v. United States
articleTitle: Judicial Interpretation of the Trade or Business Requirement in Research Tax Incentives: An Exhaustive Analysis of Zink v. United States and its Modern Progeny
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
subject: Section 174 Research Expenditures
summary: Zink v. United States, 929 F.2d 1015 (5th Cir. 1991), is a Fifth Circuit R&D tax case holding that passive investors who finance outsourced research on aircraft components cannot deduct Section 174 research expenditures. Taxpayers must show an existing trade or business or a realistic prospect of entering one; contract research cannot substitute for the taxpayer's own business.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

In Zink v. United States, 929 F.2d 1015 (5th Cir. 1991) (per curiam), the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit addressed a foundational threshold question in federal research taxation: whether individuals who finance outsourced research and development (R&D) for isolated product components, while granting nonexclusive manufacturing licenses to the promoters and exercising no control over the research or its commercialization, satisfy the "in connection with [a] trade or business" requirement of Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174. Reversing the United States District Court for the Western District of Louisiana, the Fifth Circuit held that the taxpayers were passive investors rather than active participants in a trade or business, and that they lacked any "realistic prospect" that they would ever enter a trade or business involving the development of aircraft components, the taxpayers having presented no evidence that any such prospect existed. Consequently, the court disallowed the taxpayers' claimed research and experimentation (R&E) deductions in their entirety.
The Taxpayers' Claim and Contractual Architecture

The plaintiffs-appellees, Dr. William L. Zink and Frances P. Zink, were a married couple residing in Louisiana. Dr. Zink was a surgeon who retired from his medical practice in December 1981. Having accumulated a substantial sum of oil royalty income, the Zinks sought to invest that sum during 1981 and 1982, and their accountant presented them with investments in paper pulping, oil drilling, and real estate in addition to the aircraft programs. At trial, Mrs. Zink testified that she and her husband investigated aircraft development programs promoted by Tri-Liner International, Ltd. (Tri-Liner) and Sea Star Industries, Ltd. (Sea Star) because they wanted to invest a large sum of oil royalty income, that they chose these specific programs because they lived in an oil area and the programs related to the oil business, and that they had never participated in this type of investment before.

In 1981 and 1982, the Zinks entered into two separate research and development agreements with Tri-Liner and Sea Star to finance the research and development of specific component parts for two amphibian aircraft: the left and right wings of the single-engine Avalon 680 (Tri-Liner, 1981) and the rudder parts of the twin-engine Avalon "Sea Star 2" (Sea Star, 1982). Lawrence Matanski, a licensed pilot involved in aircraft design, served as president and general manager of Tri-Liner, Sea Star, and Airmaster, Inc. (Airmaster), a subsidiary of Tri-Liner. The transaction was structured as a "purchase agreement" under which the Zinks became owners of all right, title, and interest in the plans, specifications, and technological information resulting from the research and development of their discrete airplane components; the agreement itself acknowledged that no public market existed for these rights and that it might not be possible to sell or dispose of them.

Under the contractual framework executed by the Zinks, Tri-Liner and Sea Star delegated the actual R&D work to Airmaster, which in turn either performed the aircraft component research in-house or subcontracted the engineering work to outside individuals and entities. Simultaneously, the purchase agreements required the Zinks to enter into separate licensing agreements granting Tri-Liner and Airmaster (for the wing components) and Airmaster (for the rudder components) a nonexclusive worldwide right and license to manufacture, sell, and install the components, in exchange for royalties of $1,849 and $1,417, respectively, per finished aircraft sold. As consideration under the two research agreements, the Zinks paid Tri-Liner $92,000 in cash and executed a $184,000 promissory note payable in December 1991, and paid Sea Star $47,234 in cash and executed a $94,466 promissory note payable in December 1992. On Schedule C of their federal income tax returns for 1981 and 1982, the Zinks claimed immediate Section 174 R&E deductions of $276,000 and $141,700, respectively, equal to the combined total of their cash outlays and the full face value of the promissory notes executed in favor of Tri-Liner and Sea Star.

Although a prototype Avalon 680 aircraft was eventually built and flight tested, obtained Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) operating licenses for research and development purposes, and received coverage in aviation magazine articles, orders for the Avalon 680 were insufficient to justify its production (although orders had been made for the Avalon Sea Star 2), and the Zinks never received any royalty payments or income from the programs. Following the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) audit and disallowance of their deductions, the Zinks made only two installment payments of $18,400 each on the Tri-Liner promissory note and two payments of $9,446 each on the Sea Star promissory note, and these were the only payments ever made on either note. To finance production of the Avalon 680 and Sea Star 2, the research programs were merged into a new corporation, Avalon, which Corniche Resources then purchased; participants, including the Zinks, were offered Avalon stock equivalent to the price they had paid for their research and development rights and were required to pay the balance of their Tri-Liner and Sea Star notes by returning an equivalent amount of that stock to the holder of the notes. The Zinks accepted this offer, exchanging their research agreements and royalty rights for stock that they used to pay off their outstanding promissory notes, and they made no effort to sell either the research and development or the aircraft components before doing so.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Procedural History

Upon examination, the IRS disallowed the Zinks' 1981 and 1982 Section 174 deductions in full, and in the ensuing litigation the government advanced two grounds: (1) that the Zinks were not engaged in the trade or business of developing or marketing aircraft components, and (2) that the Zinks had not established that the research and development of their component parts was completed in the years for which the deductions were taken. The Zinks paid the resulting additional $125,178 in taxes and interest and filed a claim for refund of that amount. After the IRS denied the refund claim, the Zinks initiated a tax refund suit against the United States in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana.

Following a two-day bench trial on March 13 and March 14, 1989—at which Mrs. Zink, the Zinks' accountant, and Lawrence Matanski testified on the taxpayers' behalf—the district court ruled in favor of the taxpayers. The district court found that the Zinks had invested in the programs in a businesslike manner with the intention of making a profit, concluded that they were not merely investors, and held that their activities in connection with the airplane component programs were "sufficiently substantial and regular to constitute a business" under IRC Section 174.

Before reaching the substantive tax merits on appeal, the Fifth Circuit raised on its own a question of appellate jurisdiction: whether the government had filed its notice of appeal within the 60-day period that Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(1) requires when the United States is a party. After initially entering an opinion and judgment on December 18, 1989 (the December Judgment), which it later removed from the record and placed under seal by a minute order of January 12, 1990, the district court entered, on January 11 and January 12, 1990, respectively, a "Substituted Opinion" and a "Substituted Judgment" (the January Judgment) granting judgment to the Zinks and awarding costs, but omitting the specific dollar figure of the tax refund. At the government's request (by letter dated March 7, 1990), the district court entered a further judgment on March 12, 1990 (the March Judgment) awarding the Zinks $125,602 plus interest as provided by law and $60 in costs; the government filed its notice of appeal on May 9, 1990—more than 60 days after the December and January Judgments but within 60 days of the March Judgment—so the dispute was over whether the government's notice of appeal was timely. Applying United States v. F. & M. Schaefer Brewing Co., 356 U.S. 227 (1958), the Fifth Circuit—after reiterating, under Offshore Production Contractors Insurance Co. v. Republic Underwriters, 910 F.2d 224 (5th Cir. 1990), that a judgment is final when it terminates litigation on the merits and leaves the court with nothing to do except execute the judgment, and that an immaterial revision does not extend the time to appeal—focused on the essential content of a money judgment. Quoting Schaefer Brewing, the court explained that, although no particular form of words is required, a final judgment for money must, at least, determine, or specify the means for determining, the amount of the judgment. Rejecting the Zinks' argument that the March revision was immaterial because the refund amount was uncontroverted and they had plainly won all of their claim, the court held that because the December and January Judgments did not specify the amount of the judgment, neither was final; the March Judgment was the final judgment, and the government's appeal was therefore timely.
Governing Statutory Framework and Interplay with IRC Section 41

The substantive dispute in Zink centers on IRC Section 174(a)(1), which during the years at issue permitted a taxpayer to treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year "in connection with his trade or business" as currently deductible expenses rather than capitalizable costs. Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(2) further provides that Section 174 applies not only to costs incurred for research undertaken directly by the taxpayer, but also to research or experimentation carried on "in his behalf by another person or organization".

In U.S. federal tax jurisprudence, the interpretation of the "in connection with [a] trade or business" standard under Section 174 was reshaped by the U.S. Supreme Court in Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974). Prior to Snow, decisions such as Stanton v. Commissioner, 399 F.2d 326 (5th Cir. 1968), had restrictively equated Section 174 with IRC Section 162, requiring a taxpayer to be actively producing or selling goods or services at the time the research expenses were incurred. In Snow, the Supreme Court contrasted the narrower "carrying on any trade or business" phrasing of Section 162 with the broader "in connection with his trade or business" language of Section 174. The Supreme Court held that Congress enacted Section 174 to equalize tax treatment between established corporations and nascent, pre-operational startups whose sole activity during the developmental phase is the research itself.

However, Snow did not eliminate the statutory trade or business requirement altogether. For modern U.S. tax practitioners, the principles articulated in Zink govern two intertwined statutory regimes in the Internal Revenue Code. With respect to research and experimental deductions under IRC Sections 174 and 174A, following the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA)—which mandated five-year amortization for domestic R&E and fifteen-year amortization for foreign R&E for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021—Congress enacted the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 (Public Law 119-21). This legislation added IRC Section 174A, restoring immediate deductions for domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, while retaining fifteen-year amortization for foreign research under Section 174. Under both Section 174 and Section 174A, the expenditure must be incurred "in connection with" the taxpayer's trade or business.

Simultaneously, the federal research and development tax credit under IRC Section 41—originating in 1981 and made permanent in 2015—applies a stricter nexus requirement while incorporating Section 174 by direct statutory cross-reference. First, under IRC Section 41(b)(1), Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)—comprising in-house wages, supplies, computer leasing costs, and 65% of eligible contract research expenses under Section 41(b)(3)—must be paid or incurred by the taxpayer "in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer". Second, under the four-part test of IRC Section 41(d)(1), the foundational threshold requirement—the "Section 174 Test" under Section 41(d)(1)(A)—mandates that qualified research must be research "with respect to which expenditures may be treated as expenses under section 174". Consequently, if a taxpayer fails the trade or business nexus under Zink, both the Section 174/174A deduction and the Section 41 R&D tax credit are entirely forfeited.
The Fifth Circuit's Final Holding

Reviewing the district court's factual findings under the clearly erroneous standard and its application of tax law to those facts de novo, the Fifth Circuit reversed the judgment below. The appellate panel held that the Zinks' activities (receiving reports, keeping up with the progress of the project, visiting the plant on one occasion, and attending an exhibition of the aircraft in their hometown) were insufficient as a matter of law to establish a trade or business, and, adopting the controlling inquiry articulated in Hattier v. Commissioner, 58 T.C.M. (CCH) 1109 (1990), that a taxpayer must show a realistic prospect of entering a trade or business involving the technology being developed. Because the Zinks had never engaged in the aircraft business, admittedly were not qualified to do that type of work, neither participated in nor exercised any control over the development or marketing of the components (other than the right to withdraw their investment), and held rights only to non-interchangeable sub-component plans that had no standalone commercial value, the taxpayers presented no evidence that any realistic prospect existed that they would enter a trade or business involving the development of aircraft components. Their activities were wholly consistent with those of interested investors keeping up with the progress of their investment, so the court reversed and rendered judgment for the United States, disallowing their claims in full without reaching the government's alternative argument concerning completion of the research.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of the taxpayers' claim in Zink v. United States resulted from a convergence of structural, contractual, technical, and evidentiary failures. In evaluating R&D arrangements, federal courts look past formalistic recitals in promotional documents to examine the underlying economic reality and operational substance of the venture. Analysis of the Fifth Circuit's opinion, alongside the broader body of federal R&D case law, reveals five core legal and evidentiary deficiencies that proved fatal to the Zinks' tax position.
Failure to Satisfy the Realistic Prospect Test: Absence of Objective Intent and Operational Capability

While Snow v. Commissioner permitted pre-revenue startups to deduct R&E costs under Section 174, subsequent appellate decisions—including Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148 (7th Cir. 1988), Levin v. Commissioner, 832 F.2d 403 (7th Cir. 1987), Diamond v. Commissioner, 930 F.2d 372 (4th Cir. 1991), and Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993)—established that Snow only resolved the temporal nexus to a trade or business, not the requirement that the taxpayer actually enter a trade or business at some point. In Zink, the Fifth Circuit adopted, from Hattier v. Commissioner, 58 T.C.M. (CCH) 1109 (1990), the governing standard: a taxpayer not currently engaged in an active trade or business must demonstrate a "realistic prospect" of subsequently entering its own trade or business in connection with the fruits of the research.

To satisfy the realistic prospect test, a taxpayer bears the burden of proving two conjunctive elements at the time the expenditure is incurred: objective intent and operational capability. Objective intent requires concrete, contemporaneous evidence manifesting a bona fide entrepreneurial purpose to actively commercialize, manufacture, or market the resulting technology in a business operated by the taxpayer. Capability requires the technical, managerial, financial, and operational wherewithal to actually enter and conduct that business if the research succeeds. Courts strictly distinguish between a probability of entering a business, which satisfies Section 174, and a mere theoretical possibility, which fails as a matter of law. Moreover, as the Fifth Circuit noted in Zink, establishment of the requisite profit motive alone does not satisfy Section 174: applying the two-step inquiry of Diamond v. Commissioner, 92 T.C. 423 (1989), the court asked both whether the taxpayer had the requisite profit motive and whether the taxpayer's activities were sufficiently substantial and regular to constitute a trade or business, emphasizing under Higgins v. Commissioner, 312 U.S. 212 (1941), that the management of investments is not a trade or business however extensive it may be; indeed, the government did not challenge the district court's profit-motive finding.

In Zink, the evidentiary record refuted both objective intent and capability. First, Mrs. Zink's candid trial testimony revealed that the couple looked into the programs because they wanted to invest a large sum of oil royalty income, that they had never participated in this type of investment before, and that they did not actually participate in the business, rather than intending to launch an aerospace enterprise. Second, the Zinks—a retired surgeon and his wife, a college professor of elementary education—had admittedly never engaged in the aircraft business, testified that they were not qualified to do that type of work and lacked the professional knowledge even to identify their own components on the blueprints, and, according to their accountant, had no business activities regarding the aircraft components. Unlike the general partner in Snow, who was an experienced inventor actively participating in turning an incinerator prototype into a commercial enterprise, or the partners in Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995), who were seasoned epitaxial reactor inventors guiding the technical development and holding the capital and capability to market the reactors, the Zinks lacked any operational capacity to exploit the aircraft designs.
Impermissible Delegation of the Trade or Business Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(2)

A central legal principle addressed by the court in Zink is that Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(2) expressly authorizes deductions for contract research carried on "in [the taxpayer's] behalf by another person or organization". The Zinks, for their part, asserted that the Tri-Liner and Sea Star programs were valid business enterprises, so that research performed by Airmaster and its subcontractors on their behalf, followed by manufacture of the components under nonexclusive licenses, constituted their own business activity.

The Fifth Circuit rejected this argument, explaining, with reference to Property Growth Co. v. Commissioner, 55 T.C.M. (CCH) 1072 (1988), aff'd, 889 F.2d 1090 (8th Cir. 1989), that although the regulation permits a deduction when someone else does the work on the taxpayer's behalf, the taxpayer itself must be engaged in the trade or business, and that the presence of a valid business purpose at the level of the programs did not make the development or marketing of aircraft components the Zinks' own trade or business (relying on Hattier v. Commissioner, 58 T.C.M. (CCH) 1109 (1990), which involved another investor in the 1982 Sea Star program). As the Fifth Circuit subsequently reiterated in Harris v. Commissioner, 16 F.3d 75 (5th Cir. 1994), citing Zink, although Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(2) provides that another entity may perform research on behalf of the taxpayer, the regulation does not provide that another entity may conduct a trade or business on behalf of the taxpayer. In order to qualify for a Section 174 deduction—and by extension, a Section 41 credit for contract research under IRC Section 41(b)(3)—the existing or prospective trade or business that exploits the completed research must be the taxpayer's own business, not the business of the contractor or promoter.

In Zink, the taxpayers relied on Airmaster and its subcontractors for all of the research and granted Tri-Liner and Airmaster nonexclusive worldwide licenses to manufacture, sell, and install the components; the court found the nonexclusive provision to be boilerplate totally lacking in commercial reality, and the taxpayers presented no evidence that they participated in developing or marketing the components or exercised any control over those activities other than the right to yank their investment. By relinquishing control over both the technical development and the commercial exploitation at the inception of the transaction, the Zinks ensured that any resulting trade or business belonged exclusively to Tri-Liner, Sea Star, Airmaster, and later Avalon, Inc., reducing the Zinks to passive financiers.
Illusory Component Ownership and Failure of Business Component Integrity

In contrast to the limited partnership structures at issue in earlier Tax Court precedents disallowing Section 174 deductions to passive investors, such as Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), the promoters in Zink structured the arrangement so that the Zinks directly owned the blueprints and design plans for specific component airplane parts in their individual capacities. The Zinks argued that because they held direct legal title to the component plans and possessed the theoretical legal right to manufacture or market those components independently, they satisfied the trade or business threshold.

The Fifth Circuit dismantled this structural artifice by examining the technical and economic viability of the underlying business components. Quoting Levin v. Commissioner, 832 F.2d at 407, the Zink court held that "legal entitlements, divorced from economic incentives and business probabilities, are not enough" to establish that a taxpayer is engaged in a trade or business. Specifically, Matanski testified that each aircraft was broken into about 74 component parts to be sold to investors and that the component parts were not interchangeable with other aircraft, and the Zinks' accountant confirmed that the entire aircraft would have to be manufactured before the component parts had any value. Consequently, as the court noted, the research and development information pertaining to any single component part was useless by itself. Indeed, the purchase agreement itself acknowledged that the rights arising from the research and development could not readily be sold because no public market existed, and Mrs. Zink testified that they made no effort to sell either the research and development or the aircraft components. Their component plans could only be commercialized if integrated into the complete aircraft design owned and controlled by Matanski's entities.

In modern R&D tax practice, this failure directly implicates two critical requirements under IRC Section 41: business component identification under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B) and the substantial rights and funded research exclusions under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d). Under Section 41(d)(2)(B), a taxpayer must apply the four-part qualification test separately to each "business component"—defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Artificial fragmentation of an integrated system into non-functional, non-marketable sub-components owned by passive conduits fails to create a qualifying business component in the hands of the investor. Furthermore, to claim contract research credits or avoid the funded research exclusion, a taxpayer must retain "substantial rights" in the research results and bear the financial risk of failure. When a taxpayer's nominal ownership is restricted to a useless fragment of a larger proprietary design controlled by another entity—or is subject to licensing arrangements that lack commercial reality, whether labeled exclusive or (as in Zink) nonexclusive, or to economic compulsion to surrender the rights back to the developer—the taxpayer lacks meaningful substantial rights in the technology.
Absence of Technical Direction, Experimentation Tracking, and Contemporaneous Substantiation

In the district court, the Zinks prevailed by presenting evidence of their periodic activities monitoring the investment—such as keeping up with letters, reports, news of potential sales, and exhibition locations received through the companies' mailing lists, visiting the Seattle plant once in August 1985, and attending an exhibition of the aircraft in Louisiana; Matanski himself testified that he never met the Zinks until after the airplane flew and that, after signing the agreements, they never gave him instructions of any kind. The Fifth Circuit held that the district court erred as a matter of law in equating passive investor oversight with the "substantial and regular" operational involvement required to constitute a trade or business.

As federal courts consistently emphasize in both Section 174 and Section 41 controversies, including Lewin v. Commissioner, 335 F.3d 345 (4th Cir. 2003), and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, there is a fundamental legal distinction between passive monitoring of an investment and active technical direction, supervision, and experimentation. Receiving general status updates, reading trade press, or reviewing financial ledgers represents normal ministerial oversight undertaken by a prudent investor under IRC Section 212; it does not constitute carrying on or directing a research business.

Furthermore, although the Fifth Circuit decided the case solely on the trade or business issue and did not reach the government's alternative argument that the Zinks had not established completion of the research in the years claimed (Tri-Liner and Sea Star notified the Zinks that the research on their wing and rudder components was complete roughly one and two months, respectively, after the agreements were signed), when evaluated under the substantive technical and evidentiary standards governing R&D claims under IRC Section 174 and Section 41, the record in Zink would exhibit severe documentation deficiencies across three dimensions. First, regarding the failure to substantiate technological uncertainty under IRC Section 174 and Section 41(d)(1)(A), Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(1) and Section 41 mandate that qualifying research expenditures must be incurred to discover information that would eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of developing or improving a business component. Commercial uncertainty, financial risk, or the mere prospect of FAA regulatory certification does not establish technical uncertainty, and nothing in the record described in the opinion identifies the specific engineering uncertainties of the Zinks' assigned components; indeed, Mrs. Zink testified that, although they saw the plans and blueprints in Seattle, they lacked the professional knowledge to understand them and could not even identify their own parts on the documents. Second, regarding the lack of a documented process of experimentation under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(5), substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation involving the identification of uncertainty, the formulation of hypotheses, and the systematic evaluation of one or more alternatives through modeling, simulation, systematic trial and error, or testing. Pointing to the general fact that an overall prototype aircraft (the Avalon 680) was built and flight-tested by a third party does not substantiate how specific alternatives were evaluated for the taxpayer's discrete business component, nor does it connect specific engineering labor or supply costs to that experimentation. Third, regarding the nexus between expenditures and qualifying activities under IRC Section 6001 and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(d), taxpayers bear the burden of organizing contemporaneous records so that the IRS and the courts can link claimed wage, supply, or contract expenditures directly to qualifying research activities on identifiable business components. Broad, lump-sum contract invoices and promotional summaries disconnected from actual engineering logs fail strict substantiation standards.
Financing Distortions and Lack of Genuine Economic Risk

Finally, the financial mechanics of the Zinks' contracts undermined the economic substance of their claimed deductions. Under IRC Section 174(e) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(6), Section 174 applies to a research expenditure only to the extent that the amount is reasonable under the circumstances. Similarly, under IRC Section 41(b)(3) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e), contract research expenses are eligible only when paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement entered into prior to the performance of the research, and where the taxpayer bears the true financial risk of failure.

In Zink, the taxpayers inflated their 1981 and 1982 tax deductions by claiming the full face value of promissory notes alongside their initial cash payments. Yet the notes were not due until December 1991 and December 1992, the Zinks made no payments on them until after the IRS disallowed their deductions, and they then made only two payments of $18,400 on the Tri-Liner note and two payments of $9,446 on the Sea Star note. Ultimately, the Zinks paid off the outstanding balance of both promissory notes by returning to the noteholder an equivalent amount of the stock they received in exchange for their research agreements and royalty rights in Avalon, Inc. This circular financing structure—where debt obligations used to generate upfront tax deductions were ultimately canceled via a stock conversion into the promoter's successor corporation—is consistent with the passive investor status found by the court (Matanski himself testified that the notes were used to give an incentive to investors who did not understand much about aircraft and the risks involved), although the Fifth Circuit did not separately rule on the economic substance of the notes, having disposed of the case on the trade or business issue.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To illustrate how modern U.S. taxpayers and tax advisors must structure R&D arrangements to avoid the fatal pitfalls of Zink v. United States while satisfying the rigorous requirements of IRC Sections 174A and 41, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate comprehensive structural, contractual, and evidentiary remediation.
Case Study 1: Aerospace Propulsion Sub-Assembly Venture (Overcoming Component Fragmentation and Total Delegation)
Baseline Vulnerable Scenario

AeroCap Ventures LLC ("AeroCap"), a newly formed Delaware limited liability company taxed as a partnership, is capitalized by three high-net-worth commercial real estate developers seeking to deploy $4.5 million of passive real estate gains into the regional hybrid-electric aviation sector. AeroCap enters into a turnkey R&D and Commercialization Agreement with SkyFrame Corp. ("SkyFrame"), an established aircraft design and manufacturing company developing the "VoltAir-9," a nine-passenger hybrid-electric commuter aircraft.

Under the agreement, AeroCap pays SkyFrame $1.5 million in cash and executes a $3.0 million non-recourse promissory note to fund the development of the thermal management cowling assembly specifically contoured for the VoltAir-9 nacelle. AeroCap receives legal title to the CAD blueprints for the cowling assembly, which cannot physically fit or operate on any other aircraft airframe. Simultaneously, AeroCap grants SkyFrame an exclusive, perpetual license to manufacture and integrate the cowling into the VoltAir-9 in exchange for a 2% royalty on future aircraft sales, along with an option for SkyFrame to buy out AeroCap's blueprint rights for SkyFrame common stock. AeroCap has no employees, leases no engineering or manufacturing space, and its managers merely attend quarterly video updates where SkyFrame presents flight-test footage. AeroCap claims a $4.5 million domestic R&E deduction under IRC Section 174A and claims the IRC Section 41 R&D tax credit based on 65% of the contract payments.

Under Zink v. United States, AeroCap's Section 174A deduction and Section 41 credit will be completely disallowed on audit. AeroCap has no realistic prospect of entering a trade or business: its managers lack aerospace capability, it has outsourced both R&D and all commercial exploitation to SkyFrame under Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(2), its cowling blueprints are non-interchangeable and useless standalone, and its $3.0 million note lacks economic substance.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Establishing Operational Trade or Business Capability

To satisfy the "realistic prospect" test under Zink and Scoggins v. Commissioner—as well as the "carrying on" standard of IRC Section 41(b)(1) or the qualified small business payroll tax credit election under Section 41(h)—AeroCap must transform from a passive capital conduit into an active aerospace component operating enterprise. Prior to executing any external research contracts, AeroCap hires a full-time Chief Technology Officer (CTO) and two senior aerospace thermal engineers with documented prior experience in aviation propulsion systems, placing W-2 technical personnel directly on AeroCap's payroll in alignment with the operational capability factors recognized in Scoggins. Furthermore, AeroCap leases a light assembly and thermal-testing bay at a regional industrial park and adopts a formal, board-approved five-year commercial operating plan to become an independent Tier-2 aerospace thermal subsystem supplier serving multiple regional electric aircraft original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). Rather than passively viewing flight videos, AeroCap's CTO and internal engineers establish weekly technical design review boards, retaining sole corporate authority to dictate design specifications, material selections, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) parameters, and prototype test protocols.
Step 2: Re-Engineering Business Component Scope and Contractual Architecture

AeroCap must next eliminate the "useless single component" trap identified in Zink and the impermissible delegation of the trade or business under Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(2). Rather than funding a custom cowling contour that fits only SkyFrame's VoltAir-9 airframe, AeroCap redefines the business component under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B) as the "Modular Aviation Battery Thermal Regulation Unit (MAB-TRU 100)"—a standardized, scalable liquid-cooled thermal management sub-assembly engineered with universal mounting interfaces capable of integration across multiple commercial eVTOL and hybrid-electric commuter aircraft platforms. This functional interchangeability ensures that the R&D output possesses independent, standalone market value regardless of whether SkyFrame's specific airframe succeeds.

Simultaneously, AeroCap terminates the turnkey marketing and exclusive licensing lock-in with SkyFrame. Instead, AeroCap engages SkyFrame's engineering division—or an unrelated aerospace testing facility—strictly under a Master Services Agreement (MSA) for Contract Research pursuant to Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(2) and IRC Section 41(b)(3), while retaining all downstream manufacturing, assembly, quality assurance, and multi-customer commercial sales in-house within AeroCap's own business. Under the restructured MSA, AeroCap retains 100% exclusive legal title and substantial rights under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) to all patents, trade secrets, CAD models, and test data generated during the MAB-TRU 100 development, eliminating any pre-existing buy-out option in favor of SkyFrame. Payment under the MSA is structured strictly on a milestone-contingent basis where AeroCap bears the financial risk of technical failure, and the artificial $3.0 million non-recourse note is replaced entirely with bona fide equity capital and recourse commercial working capital actually paid or incurred during the taxable year.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Process of Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy IRC Section 41(d)(1) and IRC Section 6001 substantiation rules as articulated in Phoenix Design Group and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(d), AeroCap implements a rigorous project-based documentation protocol. At project inception, AeroCap's CTO authors a Project Initiation Charter documenting the specific capability and design uncertainties of the MAB-TRU 100—specifically, that existing air-cooled heat exchangers cannot dissipate of continuous thermal load during high-altitude climb while maintaining unit mass below and pressure drop below. Throughout development, AeroCap maintains a centralized engineering repository recording each iterative hypothesis, CFD simulation model, micro-channel cold-plate geometry alternative (such as evaluating pin-fin versus serpentine versus lattice structures), dielectric coolant formulation trial, and wind-tunnel or thermal-chamber test result, including failed iterations. Finally, AeroCap's internal engineers maintain daily project time-tracking tied to specific MAB-TRU 100 experimental tasks, while contractor invoices from SkyFrame's engineering unit are itemized by specific test protocol and engineering hour, enabling a fully substantiated W-2 wage, supply, and 65% contract QRE calculation under IRC Section 41(b) alongside immediate domestic expensing under IRC Section 174A.
Case Study 2: Subsurface Petrochemical Sensor and Formulation Venture (Overcoming Passive Investor Attribution and Funded Research Pitfalls)
Baseline Vulnerable Scenario

Dr. Evelyn Vance, an orthopedic physician with substantial passive dividend and oil-and-gas royalty income, forms "PetroSense Technologies Inc." (an S corporation) to invest in downhole chemical tracer technology for hydraulic fracturing wells—mirroring the exact oil-patch investment motivation testified to by Mrs. Zink. PetroSense enters into a "Research Sponsorship and Royalty Agreement" with GeoChem Labs, Inc. ("GeoChem"), an established oilfield services and chemical manufacturing company.

Under the agreement, PetroSense pays GeoChem $800,000 in Year 1 to develop a high-temperature fluorobenzoic acid chemical tracer ("Tracer-X7") designed to blend exclusively into GeoChem's proprietary "Frac Shield" fluid system. GeoChem conducts 100% of the laboratory synthesis, stability testing, and field trials, and retains the exclusive right to manufacture and sell Tracer-X7 to oilfield operators as an additive to Frac Shield, paying PetroSense a 3% net sales royalty. Dr. Vance has no training in organic chemistry or petroleum engineering, hires no staff at PetroSense, and spends two hours a month reviewing GeoChem's quarterly financial summaries. When Tracer-X7 encounters regulatory delays, Dr. Vance exchanges PetroSense's royalty contract for preferred shares in GeoChem. On her individual return, Dr. Vance claims flow-through Section 174A deductions and Section 41 R&D credits from PetroSense.

Under Zink v. United States, Green v. Commissioner, and Kantor v. Commissioner, PetroSense's claims will be disallowed in full. PetroSense is a passive investor shelter: a company whose sole intended activity is passively collecting royalties from an exclusive licensee—without conducting an active licensing or manufacturing business of its own—is not engaged in a trade or business under Section 174 or Section 41. Moreover, because Tracer-X7 is formulated solely as an additive to GeoChem's proprietary fluid system, PetroSense owns a non-interchangeable component with no independent market utility.
Step 1: Establishing an Active Commercialization or Licensing Trade or Business

To overcome the passive investor bar of Zink and Green, PetroSense must establish both the objective intent and operational capability to conduct an active chemical formulation and commercial supply or licensing business. Rather than acting as a passive royalty conduit, Dr. Vance structures PetroSense as an active operating corporation—or forms a bona fide operating joint venture partnership with an oilfield chemical operator where the joint venture itself actively conducts the manufacturing and sales business. PetroSense recruits a Vice President of Chemical Engineering (a Ph.D. petrophysicist and organic chemist) and a Director of Oilfield Commercial Operations with established relationships across Permian Basin exploration and production (E&P) operators. To establish indisputable trade or business continuity, PetroSense secures federal and state chemical registrations in its own corporate name, establishes supply-chain blending contracts with independent toll-blenders, and actively markets its chemical tracer portfolio directly to multiple unrelated oilfield service companies and E&P operators. Even if PetroSense elects to commercialize primarily via technology licensing rather than physical manufacturing, its commercial team conducts regular, continuous, and substantial licensing negotiations and technical support across multiple market licensees to constitute an active licensing trade or business, rather than granting a single passive lock-in license to the research contractor.
Step 2: Restructuring the Contract Research and Intellectual Property Rights

PetroSense must sever the circular arrangement with GeoChem so that any outside laboratory acts strictly as a fee-for-service Contract Research Organization (CRO) rather than the proprietor of the underlying business. First, PetroSense re-scopes the R&D project to develop an independent family of encapsulated nanoparticle hydrological tracers ("HydroTrace-NP") capable of operating in any standard slickwater, gel, or cross-linked fracturing fluid across the oil and gas industry, eliminating any technical dependency on GeoChem's proprietary fluid system and ensuring standalone market value. Second, PetroSense executes a Contract Research Service Agreement compliant with Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e) with an independent laboratory prior to the performance of any research. Under the contract, the research is performed strictly on behalf of PetroSense, with PetroSense's VP of Chemical Engineering specifying all molecular weight targets, thermal degradation thresholds, and laboratory test matrices. PetroSense retains 100% unencumbered title and exclusive substantial rights to all chemical formulations, synthesis pathways, and patent applications, with zero right for the laboratory to use, manufacture, or buy out the technology. Furthermore, PetroSense bears the full economic risk of technical failure: payments to the CRO are tied to the execution of experimental synthesis runs and autoclave stability testing protocols, with no guaranteed commercial return or equity-swap bailout clause.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Experimentation Substantiation Protocol

To ensure the HydroTrace-NP project survives IRS examination under IRC Sections 174A and 41, PetroSense institutes a comprehensive scientific documentation framework. As established in federal R&D jurisprudence, the mere commercial composition or regulatory classification of a chemical product does not establish qualification; rather, an investigation of formulation stability requires concrete evidence of the technical uncertainty, alternatives evaluated, work performed, and eligible costs. PetroSense documents the exact technical uncertainty at project inception: specifically, whether a poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) versus a silica-shell nanoparticle encapsulation method can prevent premature thermal hydrolysis of the fluorobenzoic tracer at downhole reservoir temperatures exceeding and pressures of over a 90-day residence period. Rather than relying on routine concentration measurements at a wellhead, PetroSense's VP of Chemical Engineering designs a multi-stage experimental matrix evaluating twelve distinct polymer-to-silica shell thickness ratios and three cross-linking catalysts. Contemporaneous laboratory notebooks and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) test logs record the hypothesis for each batch, the high-pressure/high-temperature (HPHT) autoclave test results, the thermal degradation failure modes of rejected batches, and the iterative chemical adjustments leading to the final formulation. Finally, PetroSense maps the W-2 wages of its VP of Chemical Engineering for direct conduct and direct supervision of research, raw chemical supplies consumed in experimental synthesis batches under IRC Section 41(b)(2), and 65% of the itemized CRO laboratory testing invoices under IRC Section 41(b)(3) directly to the HydroTrace-NP business component ledger, maintaining full substantiation under IRC Section 6001.
Conclusion and Strategic Advisory Synthesis

The Fifth Circuit's decision in Zink v. United States, 929 F.2d 1015 (5th Cir. 1991), remains a cornerstone of U.S. federal R&D tax jurisprudence. While the Supreme Court's landmark ruling in Snow v. Commissioner opened the door for pre-revenue startups to deduct research expenditures under IRC Section 174 prior to commercial sales, Zink defines the outer boundary of that privilege. A taxpayer cannot convert a passive financial investment into a qualifying research activity merely by taking direct legal title to isolated component plans or invoking the contract research provisions of Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(2).

For U.S. corporate tax directors, startup founders, joint venture architects, and R&D tax credit advisors operating under the modern IRC Section 174A and Section 41 framework, Zink establishes an enduring four-pillar compliance mandate. First, while a taxpayer may contract out technical R&D tasks to third-party laboratories or engineering firms under Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(2) and IRC Section 41(b)(3), the taxpayer cannot contract out the underlying trade or business itself; the entity claiming the Section 174A deduction or Section 41 credit must possess both the objective intent and the concrete operational capability to manufacture, market, license, or internally use the resulting technology in its own trade or business. Second, economic substance governs over nominal legal title, meaning that paper legal entitlements divorced from economic incentives and commercial probabilities fail as a matter of law whenever a taxpayer holds rights only to a non-interchangeable sub-component lacking standalone market value or encumbered by licensing arrangements lacking commercial reality (whether labeled exclusive or, as in Zink, nonexclusive), contractor lock-ins, or buy-out options. Third, active technical direction must replace passive monitoring, as reviewing financial statements, attending high-level investor briefings, or tracking trade publications constitutes passive investor oversight under IRC Section 212 rather than the direct technical supervision and hypothesis formulation required for qualifying research. Fourth, contemporaneous project-based substantiation is essential: taxpayers must organize technical and financial records around identifiable, functionally viable business components, explicitly linking bona fide, at-risk expenditures to the systematic evaluation of technical alternatives aimed at resolving capability, method, or design uncertainty to withstand IRS examination.
